intro: Explore spectral measurements of historical painting materials recorded with various instruments.
footer: Data and metadata provided for research and teaching purposes.

pigments.name: Azurite
pigments.title: Azurite
pigments.description:
**Chemical Formula**
Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2
**Period of use in Art**
Known since the 25th century BC and used until 1800.
**Description**
Azurite is a rather rare and precious pigment obtained by grinding the copper mineral of the same name. Its use has been documented since the third millennium BC, and it was used as early as the Fourth Egyptian Dynasty, although it was not widely used at the time due to its instability. In Roman times, it was described by Pliny under the name Lapis Armenium. In the Middle Ages, azurite gained importance and was used extensively.
The pigment is a basic copper carbonate, unstable and reactive, which when in contact with lime and when heated, turns into black copper oxide (tenorite, CuO), so it is not recommended for use in fresco techniques. Even when applied dry, it can cause problems as it undergoes degradation due to humidity, chloride attack, and the presence of sulfides, which lead to the formation of copper sulfide and therefore to darkening of the color.
Azurite is associated with another copper-based pigment, malachite, which is green in color. Azurite and Malachite share the same chemical nature but with a different crystal structure. When azurite is exposed to air and humid conditions, the process of transformation into malachite can be activated thanks to this reaction: 
2[2CuCO3⋅Cu(OH)2] + H2O→3 [CuCO3⋅Cu(OH)2] + CO2
Microscopically, the alteration is often observed as a green malachite overgrowth or pseudomorphic replacement on azurite particles, leading to a gradual chromatic shift from blue to green. This phenomenon is particularly relevant in wall paintings and polychrome artworks, where it represents a key degradation pathway affecting original color appearance.

pigments.name: Chrysocolla
pigments.title: Chrysocolla
pigments.description:
**Chemical Formula**
(Cu,Al)2H2Si2O5(OH)4·nH2O (variable composition)
**Period of use in Art**
From Antiquity to 17th century
**Description**
Chrysocolla is a hydrated copper silicate mineral occasionally used as a blue-green pigment. It forms together with basic copper carbonates (azurite and malachite) as a secondary deposit, slightly crystalline and on copper deposits with an encrusted appearance. The widespread use of this mineral as a pigment is uncertain, due to its variable optical characteristics and degree of crystallinity, which can make it difficult to determine its presence. Pliny, in his _Naturalis Historia_, mentions it as an ingredient used to solder gold, as suggested by its name derived from the Greek words meaning gold (chrysos) and glue (kolla).

pigments.name: Egyptian Blue
pigments.title: Egyptian Blue
pigments.description:
**Chemical Formula**
CaCuSi4O10
**Period of use in Art**
From the 3rd millennium BC until the fall of the Roman Empire.
**Description**
Egyptian blue is the first known synthetic pigment, produced by heating a mixture of silica, lime, copper compounds, and alkali. It is chemically stable and exhibits characteristic luminescence under infrared radiation, a property widely used for its identification in archaeological contexts. The chemical composition of Egyptian blue corresponds to the mineral cuprorivaite, but since it is an amorphous glass, alongside cuprorivaite there are areas with unreacted quartz and glassy areas.

pigments.name: Lapis Lazuli
pigments.title: Lapis Lazuli
pigments.description:
**Chemical Formula**
(Na,Ca)8(AlSiO4)6(S,SO4,Cl)2
**Period of use in Art**
From Antiquity until the 18th century, replaced by artificial Ultramarine
**Description**
The pigment Lapis lazuli, also called natural ultramarine, comes from the precious mineral lazurite, imported mainly from Afghanistan (hence the name _ultra_ (beyond) _maris_ (sea). The mineral is an intense blue, but when ground it produces a semi-transparent grayish-blue powder because it contains many transparent compounds. For this reason, the preparation of the pigment has been gradually refined using purification methods designed to extract the intense blue. The pigment was therefore very expensive, which is why its use in painting was often reserved for works of a certain value. Its first use in painting seems to date back to the 6th-7th century AD in Afghanistan; although the pigment was known to the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, they had the alternative of Egyptian blue and used it more as an ornamental stone.

instruments.FORS:
**FORS** (Fiber Optic Reflectance Spectroscopy)
Provides reflectance vs wavelength in the _visible/near-infrared_ range.
instruments.FT-IR:
**FT-IR** (Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy)
Measures _absorption_ in the _mid-infrared_ (wavenumber) region.
instruments.Raman:
**Raman spectroscopy**
Provides _vibrational spectra_ useful for identifying molecular species.
